A precomputed structure represents a particular state of the source data. Offline processing receives the complete query set before answers are required, so it may reorder work, sort queries by a key or batch shared computation while restoring required output order. Online processing must answer each arrival without knowing future requests, ruling out strategies that depend on that knowledge. Both models still pay their actual time and memory costs.

Sorting preserves values and multiplicities but changes positions. blocks.text: How to reason about it

One linear scan costs about 1,000 dominant checks, so q scans cost 1,000q. Sorting costs about n log2 n = 10,000 comparisons and one binary search costs about 10, so the indexed total is 10,000 + 10q. Equality gives 1,000q = 10,000 + 10q, hence q ≈ 10.1; the simplified break-even is just above ten queries.
This threshold is a dominant-operation estimate. Constants, in-place mutation, original-order requirements and storage can shift or invalidate the practical decision.

The initial structure costs O(n) if it is built before the workload. Each of u updates triggers another full O(n) rebuild, contributing O(un), and q constant-time queries contribute O(q). Total time is therefore O(n + un + q), commonly simplified to O(un + q) when u ≥ 1. The repeated rebuild term exposes why a static prefix strategy may be poor for dynamic data.
A query bound is valid only while the structure is current. Charging every required rebuild keeps correctness and cost in the same model.
